Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: At eighty years old, Mama Amina had spent much of her life as a pastor, guiding her community with wisdom and compassion. Her warm smile once radiated hope, but that light had dimmed in recent years, increasingly shadowed by the horrors of her past as a refugee. The memories of her journey from conflict to safety were vivid and haunting. Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was. She often recalled the terror of fleeing her homeland, the sounds of gunfire echoing in her ears, and the sight of weapons wielded by those who sought to harm her and her family. These memories were not just flashbacks; they forced their way into her mind uninvited, leaving her breathless and disoriented, often feeling as if the events had happened to someone else entirely. It was the sheer extremity of her experiences that led her to question their reality, whispering to herself that it could not possibly have been her life that had been so violently uprooted. With each bus ride through the city, Mama Amina felt the weight of her past pressing down on her chest. The sight of other passengers made her heart race, especially if someone made a sudden movement. She would instinctively tense up, her body preparing for a threat that was no longer present. In those moments, she transformed into someone else, a woman who watched others closely for signs of danger, who frequently glanced over her shoulder, convinced that someone might be lurking behind her. This hyper-vigilance led her to avoid crowded places entirely, as the mere thought of being surrounded by others triggered a surge of anxiety that she felt ill-equipped to manage. This hyper-vigilance made her feel more like an object than a person, reduced to a collection of fears rather than a whole human being. The feeling was deeply unfair; she had survived so much only to be haunted by her past, and the injustice of it all filled her with bitterness. To cope, Mama Amina had adopted several maladaptive strategies. She avoided discussions about her experiences, even with her husband, who had been her steadfast companion through thick and thin. Talking about the trauma felt impossible, as if doing so would unravel her completely. Instead, she would wear concealing clothing to mask her anxiety, hoping to blend in and avoid drawing attention to herself. However, this avoidance meant that the memories of her trauma had never been put anywhere; they remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left them. Seeking help from medical or psychological professionals was out of the question; the thought of sharing her pain felt overwhelming, and she feared she would not be able to handle the flood of emotions that came with revisiting those memories. These strategies did little to alleviate her sense of threat, which seemed to grow each day. Even the faintest sound could transport her back to that dreadful time, the auditory echoes of her past reverberating in her mind. Whenever she was reminded of her experiences—whether through a news story or a stranger's glance—her heart would race and her body would go rigid. The combination of feeling out of control and the knowledge that nothing had been done about the injustices she had faced left her in a state of constant agitation. Her belief that the world was fundamentally unsafe meant that even mundane occurrences could set off a cascade of memories, as she constantly scanned her environment for threats that might validate her fears. She felt trapped in a cycle of avoidance, desperately trying to manage her pain while inadvertently fueling the very fears she sought to escape. Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened. As the weeks turned into months, Mama Amina found herself caught in a self-reinforcing cycle of trauma. The more she avoided public transport and interactions with strangers, the stronger her sense of threat became. The more she felt that threat, the more her memories would intrude, accompanied by feelings of helplessness and dehumanization. "Her belief that the world was fundamentally unsafe meant that even mundane occurrences could set off a cascade of memories, as she constantly scanned her environment for threats that might validate her fears." "This vigilance transformed everyday encounters into triggers, as she became increasingly hyper-aware of her surroundings, letting minor details provoke feelings of danger that would pull her back into her traumatic memories." She became increasingly isolated, retreating further into her own world, where danger lurked in every corner. "She had convinced herself that avoiding public places and discussions about her trauma would keep her safe, but this only served to heighten her sense of threat, as she never allowed herself to experience the relief of connection or the possibility of healing." What frightened her most was the prospect of reliving the trauma, a fear that held her captive, preventing her from seeking the help she so desperately needed. "Each time those memories surged, they intertwined with her sense of threat, creating an inescapable loop that made her feel as if she were reliving the trauma all over again." Now, sitting in her small office filled with books and soft lighting, Mama Amina finally felt a flicker of hope. "However, in doing so, she inadvertently heightened her sense of threat; every time she left the house, the fear of being exposed made her feel even less safe, as though the very act of hiding confirmed her belief that she had something to fear." A gentle nudge from her husband had led her to consider counseling, a step she had long avoided. As she contemplated the possibility of sharing her story, she felt a mix of anxiety and longing. What if she opened the floodgates only to find herself drowning in memories she could not control? Yet, deep down, she hoped to reclaim her life and find solace in her faith, believing that perhaps it was time to heal the wounds that had festered for far too long. "The discomfort she felt in those moments led her to withdraw from conversations and avoid situations where those reminders might surface, believing that silence was her safest option." "Her conviction that discussing her trauma would lead to greater pain kept her silent, and this belief led her to avoid even the most supportive conversations, further entrenching her sense of isolation." "This avoidance had a paradoxical effect; as she tried to suppress her memories, they only grew stronger, echoing in her mind with a clarity that felt increasingly inescapable." "These memories often culminated in the belief that she was powerless, reinforcing a narrative of helplessness that left her feeling as though she had let the chaos of her past define her present." "This state of heightened anxiety made it almost impossible for her to suppress her memories, which would intrude with vivid clarity whenever she was on high alert, as if her body was forcing her to confront what she had tried to forget." "The time spent avoiding reminders and suppressing her memories only reinforced her sense of danger, as she had never truly tested the reality of her fears against the world around her." "This heightened state of anxiety pushed her to avoid situations where those reminders might surface, leading her to withdraw from gatherings and skip outings altogether, convinced that staying away was the only way to protect herself from further distress." "Believing that her suffering was an unending burden, she felt compelled to hide her experiences, opting for silence over the risk of vulnerability, which only deepened her isolation." "This sense of imminent danger reinforced her negative appraisals of herself, leading her to conclude that she was forever vulnerable and unable to reclaim her sense of safety." "The more she avoided others and refrained from discussing her trauma, the more her memories held power over her, returning with renewed intensity each time she felt alone." "These triggers made her increasingly fearful of being in public spaces, leading her to avoid outings altogether, as she reasoned that staying home was the only way to shield herself from that overwhelming anxiety." "Her belief that speaking about her trauma would only bring more pain kept her silent, which led her to avoid conversations with friends and family, reinforcing the very isolation that heightened her anxiety." "Each time the memories intruded, she found herself questioning her worth and safety, believing that if she couldn't escape her past, it must mean something was fundamentally wrong with her." "By avoiding situations that might trigger her memories, she inadvertently intensified them; the more she suppressed her feelings, the louder and more vivid they became in her mind." "Her avoidance strategies, meant to protect her, had only served to amplify her sense of threat; without facing her fears, she remained convinced that danger was ever-present." "The memories of her trauma would flood her mind, leading her to avoid public transport altogether, as she convinced herself that staying away was the only way to prevent those feelings from crashing over her again." "She had been avoiding any mention of her experiences for so long that when the memories finally surfaced, they were louder and more vivid than ever, as if the suppression had kept them fresh and ready to overwhelm her." "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set, perpetuated by her avoidance." "But in doing so, she inadvertently heightened her sense of threat; the more she avoided situations that reminded her of her trauma, the more convinced she became that danger was ever-present." "Her negative appraisals of the world as fundamentally unsafe meant that even mundane occurrences could trigger a cascade of anxiety, as she constantly scanned her environment for signs that her fears were justified." "This belief led her to avoid conversations with friends and family, reinforcing the very isolation that heightened her anxiety and trapped her within her memories."

  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette does not depict how her maladaptive strategies affect her memories.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not connect her maladaptive strategies to triggers (her reminders of trauma).
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not show how her maladaptive strategies contribute to her sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

These memories were not just flashbacks; they forced their way into her mind uninvited, leaving her breathless and disoriented, often feeling as if the events had happened to someone else entirely. It was the sheer extremity of her experiences that led her to question their reality, whispering to herself that it could not possibly have been her life that had been so violently uprooted. With each bus ride through the city, Mama Amina felt the weight of her past pressing down on her chest. The sight of other passengers made her heart race, especially if someone made a sudden movement. She would instinctively tense up, her body preparing for a threat that was no longer present. In those moments, she transformed into someone else, a woman who watched others closely for signs of danger, who frequently glanced over her shoulder, convinced that someone might be lurking behind her.
